name: north-south barricade line of sandbags seen from above: a long band of stacked bag tops, with the end face at the bottom
label: wasteland_ruins/barricade-v

surfaces.part: sandbag stack top band (long north-south run of bag tops)
south end face of the barricade (bag-end front)

answer.evidence: Rows 0-39 are a long band of stacked bag tops. The columns repeat a lighter-gray/brown/dark pattern with a scalloped width profile (12-16 px), so the top plane is seen from above and is clearly more than a rim. At row 40 the band ends against a distinct south end face. That face is a flat brown panel with a lighter edge at its top, a darker bottom rim at rows 46-47, and a uniform body in rows 40-45, so the front face is about 8 rows. No receding isometric side face is drawn; the dark side columns are outline only.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a narrow stack of sandbag tops, about 1.5 tiles wide, with dark brownish-grey edges. The edge pixels are 0% near-neutral, so the outline is tinted rather than a black sticker line. Each bag has a highlight and a shade, and flat coverage is only 4%, so large flat fills are not a problem. The ramps are still shallow. The whole piece uses only 8 distinct colours, giving about 4 usable steps against roughly 6 on the references' roofs and stone. It shows 7 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 on the references. By eye, the bags are repeated near-identical blobs with a single highlight dot each. They lack the per-unit shading variety of the stones in house-h112 and the grain of the roof tiles. Beside the references it looks thinner and flatter, and a careful artist would not clearly accept it as equal. In doubt, fail.

surfaces.part: sandbag stack top band (long run of bag tops)
south end face of the barricade

answer.evidence: Rows 0-39 are a long top surface of stacked bag tops. Each bag repeats a light grey top strip (L~125-134) over a brown body (L~100), with narrow width changes of 12-16 px. At about row 40 a lighter edge line separates it from the end face. The end face is a boxy front of about 8 rows (rows 40-47), with a darker base at rows 46-47. The top is clearly larger than a rim, and a front face of 3+ rows is present. The reading is 3/4 view, though the end-face edge line and shadow are only weakly marked.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin, sparse sandbag column. It has about 7 visible tones per tile against 10-12 for the references, so it is lower but not drastically. Near-flat coverage is 4% against 0% for the references. The dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline is tinted, not pure black. By eye, the bags show roughly 4 lightness steps: a light top, a mid body and a dark underside. The references show about 6 steps per material, with per-tile highlights, grain and speckle. Each bag is wrapped in a fairly uniform dark contour, and the bags are lumpy and repetitive. That reads as slightly sticker-like next to the references, which separate forms by value. Per-bag texture dots and extra highlight or shadow steps are missing. Placed beside the references, it looks flatter and thinner, so I fail it.

surfaces.part: sandbag stack top band (long N-S run of bag tops)
south end face of the barricade

answer.evidence: The main body is a long band of stacked bag tops (rows 0-38), each with a light gray highlight of 2 rows, a brown body of 3 rows and a dark shadow. That is the top surface, and it is foreshortened as a receding plane. It ends in a light edge line at about rows 37-39. Below it, rows 39-47 form a brown end face of about 9 rows, with a dark base at rows 46-47. This gives a top surface plus a front face of 3 or more rows. The right-hand dark strip is shading, not an isometric side face. The top is very long for a 3/4 view, so it reads partly as a top-down view, but the end face makes it three_quarter.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a narrow vertical stack of sandbags, not a whole building with roof, walls and door, so it does not match the reference kind. The board shows it as a small, thin prop. Stones read as individually shaded grey-brown lumps with about 4 visible light steps (highlight, mid, shadow, dark), against 5-6 in the references. The outline pixels lean brown (0% near-neutral), so they are dark material tone rather than a black sticker line. Texture is present as per-bag shading, with only 4% flat coverage. Measured visible tones per tile are 7, below the references' 12 and 10, and a thin object makes that fact less decisive. By eye it is a bit thinner and flatter than the stone wall of house-h112 and has less grain. Fail on the cautious rule (when in doubt, fail): it is lower in density and fewer shading steps than the references, and a careful artist would see it as slightly thinner.

surfaces.part: sandbag stack top band (long N-S run of bag tops)
south end face of the barricade

answer.evidence: Rows 0-39 are a long band of staggered bag tops. Each bag has a light grey 2-row highlight over 3-6 rows of brown, and the width zig-zags between 12 and 16. This reads as a horizontal surface seen from above. A light edge line at about row 40 ends the band. Below it, rows 40-47 form a grey-brown end face 8 rows tall with a dark base at rows 46-47. That is the south face, so the object has both a top and a front. There is no receding side face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a narrow prop, not a whole building, so I judged it by eye against the stone wall reference. Each sandbag is shaded individually, with a light top, a mid body and a dark underside, which gives about 5 steps. That is close to the stone wall's per-stone shading. The dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outlines lean brown and grey-brown like the adjacent material rather than forming a black sticker line. Near-flat coverage is 4%, against 0% for both references, and no large area is a single flat colour. It has 7 visible tones per tile against 10-12 for the references. That is slightly lower, but the piece is thin and sparse, and the stacked-bag lumps still carry clustered texture. A careful artist would accept it beside the stone wall without it looking clearly flatter.
